title: Grasp it rightly (306–311)
hookLine: the liar goes downward; kusa grass grasped wrongly cuts the hand
last: WELL AWAKE — A MIND THAT KEEPS RETURNING HOME.

lines: A BLADE OF GRASS CAN CUT.
cards: Pull a blade of tall grass through your fingers the wrong way, and it can slice you like paper. The grass didn't change. The way you held it did.

Pick it up by the base and pull it straight, and it comes away clean. Grab it along the edge, and it bites. In India there's a grass called kusa, sharp-edged, long used in ritual and for sitting mats.
Today's verses use it to say something about how we hold even good things.

teach.h: THE DOWNWARD COURSE BEGINS WITH A LIE.
teach.b: Chapter twenty-two is called the downward course, and it speaks bluntly about what happens after harm. It opens with lying.
The one who says what didn't happen goes downward, the text says, and so does the one who did something and says, I didn't do it.
The downward course means rebirth in painful states, which Müller translates as hell; in Buddhist teaching these states don't last forever: they end when the karma that caused them runs out.
The next verses aim at monks who wear the yellow robe but live badly. Better to swallow a red-hot iron ball, one verse says, than to eat the village's offered food while living that way.

Then verse three hundred eleven, in Max Müller's English: "As a grass-blade, if badly grasped, cuts the arm, badly-practised asceticism leads to hell." Here's the surprise. The warning isn't about bad things.
It's about good ones, held wrongly. The monk's life, the practice, the discipline, can cut you if you grab it by the edge. Held with pride, it becomes a way to feel superior.
Held with harshness, it becomes self-punishment. Held with show, it becomes a costume. For anyone learning a path, including this one, it's a useful mirror.
A daily sit, a precept, a kind act can each be held rightly, lightly and honestly, by the base.
Or they can be held by the edge. The grass is the same either way.

how: Buddhist teachers use the kusa-grass verse to warn that practice held with pride or harshness does harm; kusa grass itself was long used in India for mats and ritual, and the tradition says the Buddha sat on a bundle of it on the night of his awakening.

o: a sharp-edged grass used for ritual mats
a thorny bush that marks a sacred grove
a soft reed woven into monks' robes

games.q: match each piece of today's verses.
p: cuts the hand when grasped badly
better than food eaten in bad faith
worn by some who live badly

s: verse 311 warns only about bad deeds
it warns about a good thing, practice, held the wrong way.
in Buddhist teaching, the downward states last forever
they are painful but they end when the karma that caused them runs out.
the one who says what didn't happen, or denies what they did, goes downward.

games.q: you've kept a daily sit for months, and you catch yourself quietly looking down on friends who don't. what does verse 311 say about this?
o: nothing: a good practice can't go wrong.
quit the practice to be safe.
a good practice grasped badly cuts: loosen the grip, keep the practice.
games.why: the verse compares badly held practice to grass grasped by its edge: the grass is fine; the grip is the problem.

practice: Rest your hands open on your lap and think of one good thing you do regularly: a habit, a practice, a way you help someone.
Ask gently how you're holding it, by the base, lightly and honestly, or by the edge, with a little pride or a little harshness toward yourself; no verdict needed, just notice the grip.
Then let your hands stay open, and let the breath come and go on its own.

wordCard.voice: Kusa. A sharp-edged grass used for ritual mats: held by the edge it cuts the hand, so even a good practice, held badly, can hurt.

orig.note: Pali kusa: a sharp-edged grass used for mats and ritual; verse 311's image.

carryVoice: Your line: grasp it right. Even the good things need a careful grip. Day two hundred fourteen, done.

sources.work: The Dhammapada (Sacred Books of the East, vol. 10)
sources.q: As a grass-blade, if badly grasped, cuts the arm, badly-practised asceticism leads to hell.
